transaction_steps.why: Must happen after the transaction/lock is acquired so no other process can modify either row between the read and the eventual write -- this is exactly what SELECT ... FOR UPDATE exists for, and the pattern is already used elsewhere in this repo (backend/analytics/reconciliation_views.py, backend/accounts/views.py, others -- grep-confirmed this phase).
transaction_steps.failure_requires_rollback: Row not found (already deleted by a concurrent or prior merge) -> abort, do not proceed.
transaction_steps.invariant_after: Both PaperIDs exist and are locked for the remainder of the transaction.

transaction_steps.step: Verify both records still match the approved plan
transaction_steps.why: Must be inside, immediately after the lock -- locking then finding a mismatch and rolling back is safe and cheap; locking is what makes this check meaningful (without it, a TOCTOU gap remains between check and commit).
transaction_steps.failure_requires_rollback: Any compared field differs from what the plan recorded (see stale_plan_protection).
transaction_steps.invariant_after: The live row content is provably identical to what the plan's field_actions/journal_state/author_content_conflicts were computed from.

transaction_steps.why: Same reasoning as the previous step -- this is the mechanical implementation of that verification, not a separate concern; must be inside so a failure aborts cleanly via the same transaction.
transaction_steps.invariant_after: The plan being executed is proven to be the one currently valid for these two live rows.

transaction_steps.why: This is a property of the STORED plan object, not of live DB state -- it can and should be checked before ever opening a transaction or acquiring a lock, as a cheap early exit that avoids taking any lock for a plan that was never approved.
transaction_steps.failure_requires_rollback: N/A -- never even starts a transaction.
transaction_steps.invariant_after: No transaction opened for an unapproved plan.

transaction_steps.why: Same reasoning as execution_permitted -- this is metadata about the plan/approval record, checkable before touching the database at all.
transaction_steps.failure_requires_rollback: N/A -- never even starts a transaction.

transaction_steps.invariant_after: The uq_paper_doi_normalized constraint cannot be violated by this transaction.

transaction_steps.invariant_after: Winner's ResearchPaper row reflects exactly the field_actions/journal_state the approved plan specified -- no field this phase's plan schema didn't explicitly plan for is touched.

transaction_steps.why: Writes across multiple tables that must succeed or fail together -- this is exactly what merge_group() already does today, unchanged.

transaction_steps.invariant_after: No duplicate-key row exists in any child table for the winner PaperID.

rollback_points: Winner or loser row not found under SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (already deleted).
Live row content does not match the plan's recorded field values (staleness).
DOI re-check finds a conflict that did not exist when the plan was built.
Any child-table write fails (constraint violation not caught by the existing SAVEPOINT fallback).
Profile-preservation assertion fails (a UserID lost its link to the winner).
Any new, equivalent invariant a future executor's design adds (e.g. an AuthorNameRaw-conflict re-check, a JournalID FK-target-still-exists re-check).

stale_plan_protection.schema_evidence: ResearchPaper has NO updated-at / modified-at column of any kind (confirmed by a fresh information_schema.columns scan this phase for column names matching '%update%' or '%modif%' -- zero results across all 33 columns). A timestamp-based staleness check is therefore not directly supported by the current schema.
stale_plan_protection.recommended_approach: Content fingerprint (a deterministic hash of exactly the ResearchPaper column values, Authors rows, and dependency row-counts the plan's field_actions/journal_state/author_content_conflicts were computed from), stored alongside the generated plan, and re-computed + compared immediately after the SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the executor's transaction.
stale_plan_protection.why_this_over_alternatives: Row fingerprint/content-hash is the only one of the suggested approaches that requires zero schema change and is provably correct: it directly captures 'is this the same data the plan reasoned about', which is the actual safety property needed, rather than a proxy for it (a timestamp only proves 'something changed at some point', not 'this specific data changed'; a bare updated-timestamp column doesn't exist anyway).
what_would_need_building: A canonical serialization of the exact fields the plan already reads (RP_COLUMNS values, Authors UserID+AuthorNameRaw pairs, dependency row counts) -- deterministic ordering, deterministic value formatting.
A hash function applied to that serialization, stored as a 'plan_fingerprint' field on the generated plan JSON.
An executor-side re-fingerprint-and-compare step, inside the transaction, after the row lock and before any write.
None of this exists in the repository today -- merge_plan_generator.py's plans carry no fingerprint field currently; this is 100% new work for a future phase, not a gap in existing code.

database_row_locking.evidence: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is already used in this exact raw-cursor style elsewhere in the repository (backend/analytics/reconciliation_views.py line ~124, inside a transaction.atomic() block with connection.cursor() -- grep-confirmed this phase across 7 files total), so it is a proven, repository-native pattern directly reusable by a future executor, not a new architectural concept.
database_row_locking.role: Locking prevents a NEW concurrent modification during the transaction; it does not by itself detect that the row already changed BEFORE the transaction started -- that is what the fingerprint check is for. The two mechanisms are complementary, not alternatives.

existing_audit_table.evidence: merge_group() already INSERTs an AuditLog row (Action='paper.merge.dedup', TargetType='ResearchPaper', TargetID=<loser PaperID>, Metadata=<kept_paper_id, loser_title, loser_doi, ...>) for every loser merged. A fresh query this phase found 59 such rows already in the live database from real, historical --apply runs -- this is a proven, populated, working mechanism, not a hypothetical one.
existing_audit_table.caveat: No unique constraint enforces at most one 'paper.merge.dedup' AuditLog row per TargetID -- LogID is a bare auto-increment PK, and idx_audit_action/idx_audit_tenant_date/idx_audit_user are plain (non-unique) indexes. Idempotency is therefore NOT a database-enforced guarantee today; it would have to be an explicit executor preflight check (query AuditLog for an existing row with this TargetID before proceeding), not something the schema prevents on its own.

primary_existing_mechanism.description: dedup_papers.py's own --apply --plan path already has a real, working idempotency check: on load, it re-reads live ResearchPaper.PaperID membership and drops any plan group whose kept/loser IDs no longer exist (main(), the 'alive' filter). A loser that was already merged away is simply absent from ResearchPaper, so re-running the same plan a second time is already a safe no-op for that group today.
primary_existing_mechanism.gap: This only proves the row is GONE, i.e. 'was deleted by something' -- it does not prove it was deleted BY THIS SPECIFIC PLAN as opposed to a different, possibly conflicting later merge. Combining this existence-check with an AuditLog cross-check (above) closes that gap without inventing a new table.

idempotency_requirements.prevent_double_execution: Preflight: (1) does the loser PaperID still exist in ResearchPaper (existing mechanism); (2) does an AuditLog row with Action='paper.merge.dedup' and TargetID=<loser> already exist (existing table, new query). Both must be checked; neither alone is sufficient (see gap above).
idempotency_requirements.prevent_winner_loser_reversal: The plan JSON already names survivor/loser explicitly and unambiguously (Phase 4C/4E's plan schema: 'survivor' and 'loser' keys, not positional). A future executor must read the plan's own recorded IDs, never re-derive winner/loser at execution time from a fresh choose_keep() call -- re-deriving could disagree with the approved plan if the underlying data changed (this is exactly what stale-plan protection above catches, but as a design principle: EXECUTE the plan's decision, do not RE-DECIDE it at execution time, mirroring --apply's own documented philosophy for group-level merges: 'it doesn't re-decide it').
idempotency_requirements.prevent_execution_after_one_record_alrea: Covered by the same existence-check preflight above -- if either winner or loser PaperID is already gone, abort before opening a write transaction.
idempotency_requirements.prevent_partial_repeat_of_child_migratio: merge_group()'s own operations are already individually idempotent in isolation (INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, GREATEST()-based UPDATE, remap_simple_child()'s UPDATE-by-PaperID which becomes a no-op once already remapped) -- re-running the same merge_group() call against an already-migrated-but-not-yet-deleted state would not duplicate data. The genuine risk is not partial-repeat corruption within one merge_group() call (already safe), it's a SECOND, independent invocation racing the first without a lock -- which is exactly what the row-locking design in transaction_steps prevents.
idempotency_requirements.no_new_table_invented: Per the task's explicit instruction, no new execution-tracking table is proposed here. AuditLog plus the existing ResearchPaper-existence check are evidenced as sufficient building blocks; whether a future phase additionally wants a dedicated table (the repository does have an existing job-tracking convention, SyncJob, confirmed to exist this phase, that a future design COULD look to as precedent) is left as an open decision for a future phase, not decided here.

proposed_executor_contract.accepted_input: One previously-generated plan object (the exact JSON shape merge_plan_generator.py already produces, extended with a plan_fingerprint field per stale_plan_protection) plus a reference to a recorded human-approval event where the plan's classification is not SAFE_PLAN_CANDIDATE-with-zero-conflicts. The executor never re-detects duplicates and never re-decides survivor selection -- it only executes an already-approved plan, mirroring --apply --plan's existing philosophy exactly.
proposed_executor_contract.approval_requirements: execution_permitted must be true on the plan (today this is never true; a future, separate, out-of-scope-for-this-phase approval workflow would need to set it, e.g. an admin action that re-validates the plan is still SAFE and stamps an approval record). A plan whose classification is PLAN_REQUIRES_HUMAN_APPROVAL must carry an explicit, recorded human decision per unresolved_conflicts entry (especially journal_state=CONFLICT and any author_content_conflicts) before execution_permitted may ever be set true for it -- this executor must refuse to run otherwise, full stop.
required_preflight_checks: Recorded human approval exists where the plan's classification required one.
Both winner and loser PaperIDs still exist in ResearchPaper (existing --apply pattern).
No prior AuditLog Action='paper.merge.dedup' row for this loser PaperID (idempotency).
Plan fingerprint matches freshly-computed live-data fingerprint (staleness).
proposed_executor_contract.transaction_behavior: Exactly one transaction.atomic() per pair executed (narrower than --apply's current one-transaction-per-whole-run design, which wraps every group in a single call) -- see transaction_steps for the full ordered sequence. A narrower per-pair transaction is recommended specifically because Phase 4D/4E's evidence shows real pairs can have real, blocking-worthy conflicts discovered only at a granular level (JournalID, AuthorNameRaw); isolating each pair's transaction limits the blast radius of any single pair's unexpected failure without touching --apply's existing, already-tested, all-groups-in-one-transaction behavior for its own (unrelated) call path.
proposed_executor_contract.locking_requirements: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on both ResearchPaper rows (winner, loser) as the first statement inside the transaction, using the exact raw-cursor style already present elsewhere in this repository (backend/analytics/reconciliation_views.py and 6 other files, grep-confirmed this phase) -- not a new pattern.
proposed_executor_contract.child_migration_rules: Reuse merge_group()'s existing, unmodified logic for every dependency already classified MUST_REMAP_BEFORE_DELETE (Authors, Citations, ExternalAuthors, PaperKeywords, CitationsHistory, ReportPaperDecision.PaperID) -- do not rewrite what already works and is tested. Explicitly ADD two operations merge_group() does not perform today, gated by the plan's own journal_state/author_content_conflicts: (a) if journal_state.state == LOSER_ONLY_BACKFILL, UPDATE the winner's JournalID to the loser's value before the loser is deleted; (b) if author_content_conflicts is non-empty, REFUSE to execute (this should already be caught by execution_permitted being false for such a plan, but the executor must defensively re-check rather than trust the plan blindly, matching the existing profile-preservation-assertion philosophy of 'verify the invariant right before it would be violated, not just at plan-generation time').
proposed_executor_contract.conflict_behavior: Any conflict discovered fresh at execution time that the plan did not already account for (a fingerprint mismatch, a new AuthorReviewQueue row that didn't exist when the plan was built, a JournalID that changed) aborts the transaction entirely -- no partial application, no best-effort merge, no silent skip-and-continue. This matches the existing profile-preservation-assertion pattern in merge_group() exactly: raise, and let transaction.atomic() roll back everything.
proposed_executor_contract.audit_requirements: Continue using AuditLog exactly as merge_group() does today (Action='paper.merge.dedup', TargetType='ResearchPaper', TargetID=loser, Metadata capturing kept_paper_id/loser fields) -- no new audit mechanism needed, this one is proven (59 real historical rows) and already correctly ordered (written before the loser delete, inside the same transaction). Additionally record, in Metadata, the plan_fingerprint that was verified and the approval reference that authorized this specific execution, so a future audit can answer 'which approved plan, exactly, produced this merge' -- a field the current Metadata shape does not carry, since no plan-approval concept existed before this phase's design.
proposed_executor_contract.idempotency_behavior: Preflight-checked, not database-enforced (see idempotency_requirements) -- the executor must refuse to re-run against a loser PaperID that either no longer exists in ResearchPaper or already has a 'paper.merge.dedup' AuditLog row, treating both as 'already done, not an error, but also not something to repeat.'
proposed_executor_contract.rollback_guarantees: Everything inside the one per-pair transaction rolls back atomically on any failure (Postgres/Django transaction.atomic() semantics, already relied upon throughout dedup_papers.py) -- there is no partial-merge state reachable from a failed execution, matching --apply's existing guarantee for its own, coarser-grained transaction today.
proposed_executor_contract.post_merge_verification: Re-run the existing profile-preservation assertion (every UserID linked to either original copy is still linked to the winner) inside the transaction before COMMIT (already exists, unchanged). Additionally verify, post-commit as a separate read-only check (not inside the transaction, since it's confirming durable state): the loser PaperID is absent from ResearchPaper; the winner's JournalID matches the plan's planned final value; no orphaned child-table row references the now-deleted loser PaperID in any of the 7 dependency tables from the dependency_map.
